=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of the Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

## Threshold point: the "FINAL / market standard" preamble

The Seller's preamble says these positions are "standard", "settled at principal level" and "not intended to be re-opened." That is the Seller's advocacy, not an agreed fact, and it should not limit our review.

- **Settlement status:** Please confirm with your principals whether anything was actually agreed. If something was, we should know exactly what, because several of these positions would be unusual to concede.
- **Market terms:** Even where a figure is within a "market" range, what matters is how the terms work together. Here, a broad general disclosure plus a constructive-knowledge bar plus a deductible basket plus a cap that applies to every claim would leave the warranties of little practical value.
- **Our response:** We should reply in our mark-up without accepting the "FINAL" characterisation.

I have only seen the Seller's update and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying DD documents (DD-002 to DD-012). Several points below need checking against those documents.

---

## Part A: Transaction-specific issues (highest priority)

These involve identified, quantifiable exposures. The Seller is either pushing them onto us or leaving them unresolved.

### 1. Riverlark facility (about AUD 3.2m): release "following Completion" (Cl 2/7)
**Why it matters**
- On a debt-free/cash-free deal, this debt must be repaid out of the price at Completion.
- DD-003 has a change-of-control clause (8.1). Completion is therefore likely to trigger a default or prepayment event while the security is still in place over the company we have just bought.
- A post-Completion release leaves us holding an encumbered company, relying on the Seller's promise.
- We need to check whether Riverlark's security also covers the **shares** (for example, a share mortgage or a general security interest given by Harbourglass). If it does, this is also a **title** problem.

**Push back**
- Treat Riverlark as Indebtedness, repaid at Completion directly from the funds flow under a payout letter.
- Signed deed of release, PPSR financing change statements and return of title documents to be **Completion deliverables**.
- Lender waiver of cl 8.1 (or repayment that makes it irrelevant) to be a condition.
- Specific indemnity for any residual amount, outside the cap.

### 2. Bluefen consent (about 30% of revenue, about AUD 3.6m) (Cl 3/6.3)
**Why it matters**
- The Seller proposes only "reasonable endeavours". It also wants the condition treated as satisfied merely on delivery of "the counterparty's written consent", even though the clause 11.3 conditions have not been met.
- Losing Bluefen would put a large part of the valuation at risk.
- The Disclosure Letter confirms that no final consent and no evidence of the 11.3 conditions has been provided.

**Push back**
- Condition precedent requires an **unconditional** written consent (or one whose conditions are acceptable to the Buyer), in a form satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably, with every clause 11.3 condition satisfied.
- Condition waivable **only by the Buyer**.
- Seller to use "all reasonable endeavours" (or best endeavours) to obtain it.
- Consider additional protection: a customer-specific warranty (no notice of termination or non-renewal), a walk right, and price protection such as an escrow or an earn-out-style adjustment if Bluefen terminates within an agreed period.

### 3. Completion bonuses (AUD 420,000 plus on-costs): "a matter for the Seller"
**Why it matters**
- These bonuses are the **Company's** liability as employer. They are not the Seller's.
- If they are left out of the funds flow, we effectively pay for them on top of the AUD 24m.
- The Disclosure Letter is silent on PAYG withholding, superannuation, payroll tax and workers' compensation on-costs, which are likely to apply.

**Push back**
- Bonuses and all on-costs to be Transaction Expenses / Indebtedness and deducted from the price.
- Bonuses paid through Company payroll at or immediately after Completion, funded by the deduction.
- Specific indemnity for any shortfall, including employment tax.

### 4. Ironquay IP (Cl 11.1): indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment
**Why it matters**
- Under DD-004 cl 7.3, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials passes only on **cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**.
- DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 still open. There is no evidence of payment and no confirmatory assignment.
- If the materials form part of the product, the Company may not own core IP.
- An indemnity limited to the payment amount does not cover loss of ownership, re-development costs, injunction risk or third-party claims.

**Push back**
- The AUD 180,000 to be paid before Completion (with evidence of cleared funds) or deducted from the price.
- An executed confirmatory **IP assignment from Ironquay** to be a Completion deliverable or condition.
- The indemnity to cover all Loss arising from any failure of the Company to own the SOW3 materials, with no disclosure or knowledge qualification, sitting outside the general cap and basket, and with a longer survival period.

### 5. DD-006 data export incident: "not expected to be material" (Cl 4.6 / Sch 6)
**Why it matters**
- About 1,240 personal records were sent by link to an unintended external address.
- Paperbark appears to be above the AUD 3m turnover threshold (Bluefen's AUD 3.6m is about 30% of revenue). If so, it is likely an APP entity under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth).
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach generally must complete a reasonable assessment within **30 days**.
- The incident was known by 22 September and the investigation was still "preliminary". It is now 5 November, so the assessment period may already have **lapsed**. That is a compliance issue in itself.
- Penalties and regulatory scrutiny under the amended Privacy Act are significant.
- Calling it "not material" is the Seller's opinion, and Schedule 6 disclosure would be used to qualify the privacy warranties.

**Push back**
- Seller to give us now the incident timeline, forensic findings, access logs and its NDB assessment.
- A pre-Completion covenant to finish the assessment and make any required OAIC or individual notifications, in consultation with the Buyer.
- A **specific indemnity** for all Loss from the incident, including regulatory penalties to the extent the law permits indemnity, notification and remediation costs, and third-party claims. It should not be qualified by disclosure or Buyer knowledge, should sit outside the cap and basket, and should survive at least 3 to 4 years.
- Consider a retention or escrow amount.

### 6. Sandbar renewals (3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000): "ordinary course"
**Why it matters**
- The Disclosure Letter itself says the three are "related" and should be "read together for timing/scope." The Seller's description as ordinary-course costs is not supported by it.
- Three linked commitments around the time of the sale are a warning sign: possible contract-splitting to avoid approval thresholds, a related party of the Seller, or value leakage.

**Push back**
- Request the contracts and the approval trail. Confirm whether Sandbar is related to Harbourglass or its personnel, and whether the renewals are terminable, prepaid or accrued.
- If related-party or non-arm's-length: treat as Leakage or Indebtedness, or require termination before Completion.
- Add a specific warranty that the renewals are arm's-length, approved and terminable without penalty.
- Tighten the conduct-of-business covenants so that new commitments above a threshold, say AUD 50,000, need Buyer consent.

### 7. Title (DD-012 register only)
**Why it matters**
- The Disclosure Letter expressly says the register "does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification."
- A register entry alone does not establish unencumbered title. The Seller is also trying to cap the title warranty (see item 9 below).

**Push back**
- Full, uncapped title and capacity warranties covering legal and beneficial ownership, no Encumbrances, no options or rights to issue shares, and fully paid shares.
- We should run our own ASIC, PPSR and insolvency searches against both the Seller and the Company.
- Completion deliverables: signed share transfers, share certificates and releases of any share security.

### 8. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
**Why it matters**
- The Seller characterises these as a notification-only obligation and an assignment restriction that the share sale does not trigger.
- These may well be correct, but they are the Seller's readings.

**Push back**
- We should read the clauses ourselves for change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording.
- Add a warranty that no consent is required, and a covenant to give the lease notification on time.

---

## Part B: The limitations regime

### 9. Fundamental warranties capped at 20% and 18 months
This is not acceptable. Title and capacity are the core of what we are buying. If title fails, our loss is the entire AUD 24m.

**Push back**
- Fundamental warranties capped at 100% of the price.
- Survival of at least 6 to 7 years, or the statutory limitation period.
- Fundamental warranties excluded from the de minimis and basket.

### 10. Tax and IP folded into the general regime
**Tax**
- Tax exposure typically appears well after 18 months, because ATO amendment periods are commonly 2 to 4 years and are unlimited for fraud or evasion.

**Push back on tax**
- A separate tax indemnity covering all pre-Completion tax, including payroll tax and superannuation guarantee charge.
- Cap at 100% of the price, with survival of 5 to 7 years.
- No basket, and not qualified by disclosure.

**IP**
- IP is likely the main value driver for a SaaS business.

**Push back on IP**
- A higher cap (for example 50 to 100% of the price) and longer survival (for example 3 years).

### 11. Liability cap: 20% (AUD 4.8m) for general warranties
**Position**
- 20% is within a range commonly seen for general warranties. The figure alone is not the main battle, provided everything in Part A and items 9 and 10 sits **outside** it.

**Push back**
- The cap should apply to general warranty claims **only**.
- Carve out fraud, wilful concealment, fundamental warranties, the tax indemnity, specific indemnities, covenant breaches, Leakage and price adjustments.
- If a W&I policy is being considered, the structure changes: the Seller's cap drops, but we need the insurer's exclusions (likely including the known DD-006, Ironquay and Bluefen issues) backed by specific Seller indemnities.

### 12. Thresholds (Cl 12.2): de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000, excess only
**Why it matters**
- The basket is about 1.04% of the price and is structured as a **deductible**, so we always absorb the first AUD 250,000.

**Push back**
- A **tipping** basket (once exceeded, we recover from the first dollar), at about 0.5% (AUD 120,000).
- De minimis of AUD 10,000 to 15,000.
- Related or similar claims aggregated for de minimis purposes.
- No thresholds applying to fundamental warranties, tax, indemnities or covenants.

### 13. Time limits: 18 months, applying to "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"
**Why it matters**
- This default is a drafting trap. Any category we forget to carve out expressly would fall under 18 months.

**Push back**
- The 18-month period to apply **only** to general Warranty Claims. Consider 24 months so that at least two audit cycles are covered.
- Each other category to have its own stated period.
- Notification requirements to be satisfied by a notice giving reasonable detail. Proceedings to be issued within 6 to 9 months of notice.

### 14. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (Cl 9.3/12.8/20.5)
**Why it matters**
- As drafted, this would cap even claims based on fraud.

**Push back**
- Express carve-out for fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller or its officers, employees and advisers.
- Exclusive remedy not to limit specific performance, injunctions, termination rights or indemnities.
- Note: under NSW/Australian law, parties generally cannot contract out of ACL s 18 (misleading or deceptive conduct). Non-reliance clauses can still weigh heavily against a claim on the evidence, so we should not accept broad non-reliance wording just because it may be unenforceable.

---

## Part C: Disclosure and knowledge

### 15. General disclosure of the data room and public records (Sch 7 / DL 1.1–1.2)
**Why it matters**
- This would qualify every warranty against everything in the data room and every public register, whether or not we could reasonably have spotted it.
- The cut-off of 22 September 2026 is now over six weeks old.

**Push back**
- Only **specific** disclosures in the Disclosure Letter qualify the warranties.
- A **fair disclosure** standard: sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and financial effect of the matter.
- Data room disclosure, if conceded at all, limited to documents in an **agreed index annexed to the SPA**, with an archived copy (USB) delivered at signing.
- Public register disclosure limited to specified searches on a specified date.
- No disclosure against fundamental warranties, the tax indemnity or specific indemnities.
- Updated disclosure at signing and any bring-down, with a Buyer termination right for new material matters.
- DL 1.4 ("no admission") is acceptable, but it should not dilute the specific indemnities.

### 16. Buyer knowledge bar (Cl 8.3)
**Why it matters**
- This is the most damaging clause in combination with item 15. It covers the knowledge of our **advisers** and anything "discoverable", which amounts to constructive knowledge.
- On its face, it would arguably bar claims on every issue in this memo, because we have now identified them all.

**Push back**
- Primary position: delete it and include an express pro-sandbagging clause (our rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge).
- Fallback: limited to the **actual** knowledge of named individuals of matters **fairly disclosed** in the Disclosure Letter.
- In any case, it must never apply to specific indemnities, the tax indemnity or fundamental warranties.

---

## Part D: Price mechanics

### 17. Funds flow and the debt-free/cash-free definitions
**Why it matters**
- The Seller says the funds flow "reflects the agreed price mechanics" while leaving out the bonuses.

**Push back**
- Indebtedness and Transaction Expenses to expressly include:
  - the Riverlark payout, including break costs and fees;
  - the AUD 420,000 bonuses plus all on-costs;
  - the unpaid Ironquay AUD 180,000;
  - any related-party Sandbar amounts;
  - accrued but unpaid tax;
  - Seller transaction costs borne by the Company.
- Completion accounts or a locked-box Leakage covenant, as applicable, with a dollar-for-dollar indemnity.
- Consider a retention or escrow amount (for example 5 to 10%) for the known issues.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Buyer recommendation | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Riverlark AUD 3.2m | Release post-Completion | Repay from price at Completion; deed of release and PPSR discharges as deliverables; check share security | Critical |
| 2 | Bluefen (30% revenue) | Reasonable endeavours; any written consent suffices | Unconditional, Buyer-satisfactory consent with 11.3 conditions met; Buyer-only waiver; customer protection | Critical |
| 3 | Bonuses AUD 420k | Seller's matter; not in funds flow | Deduct from price plus all on-costs; specific indemnity | Critical |
| 4 | Ironquay IP | Indemnity limited to SOW3 payment | Payment or deduction plus confirmatory assignment as a deliverable; full IP-loss indemnity outside cap | Critical |
| 5 | DD-006 privacy incident | "Not material" | Full information now; finish NDB assessment and notify; uncapped/unqualified specific indemnity; retention | Critical |
| 6 | Fundamental/title | Same 20%/18 months | 100% cap; 6–7 years; no thresholds; own ASIC/PPSR searches | Critical |
| 7 | Buyer knowledge (8.3) | Constructive and adviser knowledge bars claims | Delete and add pro-sandbagging; fallback: actual knowledge of named persons of fairly disclosed matters | Critical |
| 8 | General disclosure | Whole data room plus public records | Specific, fair disclosure; annexed index; no disclosure against indemnities, tax or fundamentals | High |
| 9 | Limitations apply to all claims | Yes, including fraud | Carve out fraud and wilful concealment, indemnities, covenants, Leakage | High |
| 10 | Tax / IP | General regime | Tax indemnity (100%, 5–7 years); higher IP cap and survival | High |
| 11 | Sandbar AUD 330k | Ordinary course | Diligence on related-party status; Leakage treatment or termination; tighter interim covenants | High |
| 12 | Basket | AUD 250k deductible | About AUD 120k tipping; de minimis AUD 10–15k with aggregation | Medium |
| 13 | Time limits | 18 months for all claims by default | 18–24 months for general warranties only; separate periods for each other category | Medium |
| 14 | General cap 20% | AUD 4.8m on all claims | Acceptable for general warranties only, if carve-outs are agreed | Medium |
| 15 | Lease / Mossvale | No consent needed | Verify the clauses ourselves; add warranty and notice covenant | Medium |

## Suggested next steps

1. **Confirm settlement status:** Check with the principals whether any of these points were genuinely settled. Do not accept the "FINAL" label in correspondence.
2. **Send an information request:** DD-006 forensic and NDB material; Riverlark security documents and payout figure; Bluefen correspondence on 11.3; Ironquay payment status; Sandbar contracts and relationship; bonus terms and on-cost calculation.
3. **Run our own searches:** ASIC, PPSR and insolvency searches on Harbourglass and Paperbark.
4. **Decide on W&I:** If W&I insurance is on the table, decide now, because it reshapes the cap and limitations negotiation. Known issues will need Seller specific indemnities regardless.
5. **Prepare the mark-up:** Lead with the Part A items as the commercial priorities. Treat the limitations regime (Parts B and C) as an integrated package rather than clause by clause.

I can prepare the SPA mark-up language for the specific indemnities, the fair-disclosure clause and the pro-sandbagging clause if helpful.

- The Disclosure Letter itself says the three are "related" and should be "read together for timing/scope." The Seller's description as ordinary-course costs is not supported by it.
- Three linked commitments around the time of the sale are a warning sign: possible contract-splitting to avoid approval thresholds, a related party of the Seller, or value leakage.

**Push back**
- Request the contracts and the approval trail. Confirm whether Sandbar is related to Harbourglass or its personnel, and whether the renewals are terminable, prepaid or accrued.
- If related-party or non-arm's-length: treat as Leakage or Indebtedness, or require termination before Completion.
- Add a specific warranty that the renewals are arm's-length, approved and terminable without penalty.
- Tighten the conduct-of-business covenants so that new commitments above a threshold, say AUD 50,000, need Buyer consent.

### 7. Title (DD-012 register only)
**Why it matters**
- The Disclosure Letter expressly says the register "does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification."
- A register entry alone does not establish unencumbered title. The Seller is also trying to cap the title warranty (see item 9 below).

**Push back**
- Full, uncapped title and capacity warranties covering legal and beneficial ownership, no Encumbrances, no options or rights to issue shares, and fully paid shares.
- We should run our own ASIC, PPSR and insolvency searches against both the Seller and the Company.
- Completion deliverables: signed share transfers, share certificates and releases of any share security.

### 8. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
**Why it matters**
- The Seller characterises these as a notification-only obligation and an assignment restriction that the share sale does not trigger.
- These may well be correct, but they are the Seller's readings.

**Push back**
- We should read the clauses ourselves for change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording.
- Add a warranty that no consent is required, and a covenant to give the lease notification on time.

## Part B: The limitations regime

### 9. Fundamental warranties capped at 20% and 18 months
This is not acceptable. Title and capacity are the core of what we are buying. If title fails, our loss is the entire AUD 24m.

**Push back**
- Fundamental warranties capped at 100% of the price.
- Survival of at least 6 to 7 years, or the statutory limitation period.
- Fundamental warranties excluded from the de minimis and basket.

### 10. Tax and IP folded into the general regime
**Tax**
- Tax exposure typically appears well after 18 months, because ATO amendment periods are commonly 2 to 4 years and are unlimited for fraud or evasion.

**Push back on tax**
- A separate tax indemnity covering all pre-Completion tax, including payroll tax and superannuation guarantee charge.
- Cap at 100% of the price, with survival of 5 to 7 years.
- No basket, and not qualified by disclosure.

**IP**
- IP is likely the main value driver for a SaaS business.

**Push back on IP**
- A higher cap (for example 50 to 100% of the price) and longer survival (for example 3 years).

### 11. Liability cap: 20% (AUD 4.8m) for general warranties
**Position**
- 20% is within a range commonly seen for general warranties. The figure alone is not the main battle, provided everything in Part A and items 9 and 10 sits **outside** it.

**Push back**
- The cap should apply to general warranty claims **only**.
- Carve out fraud, wilful concealment, fundamental warranties, the tax indemnity, specific indemnities, covenant breaches, Leakage and price adjustments.
- If a W&I policy is being considered, the structure changes: the Seller's cap drops, but we need the insurer's exclusions (likely including the known DD-006, Ironquay and Bluefen issues) backed by specific Seller indemnities.

### 12. Thresholds (Cl 12.2): de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000, excess only
**Why it matters**
- The basket is about 1.04% of the price and is structured as a **deductible**, so we always absorb the first AUD 250,000.

**Push back**
- A **tipping** basket (once exceeded, we recover from the first dollar), at about 0.5% (AUD 120,000).
- De minimis of AUD 10,000 to 15,000.
- Related or similar claims aggregated for de minimis purposes.
- No thresholds applying to fundamental warranties, tax, indemnities or covenants.

### 13. Time limits: 18 months, applying to "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"
**Why it matters**
- This default is a drafting trap. Any category we forget to carve out expressly would fall under 18 months.

**Push back**
- The 18-month period to apply **only** to general Warranty Claims. Consider 24 months so that at least two audit cycles are covered.
- Each other category to have its own stated period.
- Notification requirements to be satisfied by a notice giving reasonable detail. Proceedings to be issued within 6 to 9 months of notice.

### 14. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (Cl 9.3/12.8/20.5)
**Why it matters**
- As drafted, this would cap even claims based on fraud.

**Push back**
- Express carve-out for fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller or its officers, employees and advisers.
- Exclusive remedy not to limit specific performance, injunctions, termination rights or indemnities.
- Note: under NSW/Australian law, parties generally cannot contract out of ACL s 18 (misleading or deceptive conduct). Non-reliance clauses can still weigh heavily against a claim on the evidence, so we should not accept broad non-reliance wording just because it may be unenforceable.

## Part C: Disclosure and knowledge

### 15. General disclosure of the data room and public records (Sch 7 / DL 1.1–1.2)
**Why it matters**
- This would qualify every warranty against everything in the data room and every public register, whether or not we could reasonably have spotted it.
- The cut-off of 22 September 2026 is now over six weeks old.

**Push back**
- Only **specific** disclosures in the Disclosure Letter qualify the warranties.
- A **fair disclosure** standard: sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and financial effect of the matter.
- Data room disclosure, if conceded at all, limited to documents in an **agreed index annexed to the SPA**, with an archived copy (USB) delivered at signing.
- Public register disclosure limited to specified searches on a specified date.
- No disclosure against fundamental warranties, the tax indemnity or specific indemnities.
- Updated disclosure at signing and any bring-down, with a Buyer termination right for new material matters.
- DL 1.4 ("no admission") is acceptable, but it should not dilute the specific indemnities.

### 16. Buyer knowledge bar (Cl 8.3)
**Why it matters**
- This is the most damaging clause in combination with item 15. It covers the knowledge of our **advisers** and anything "discoverable", which amounts to constructive knowledge.
- On its face, it would arguably bar claims on every issue in this memo, because we have now identified them all.

**Push back**
- Primary position: delete it and include an express pro-sandbagging clause (our rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge).
- Fallback: limited to the **actual** knowledge of named individuals of matters **fairly disclosed** in the Disclosure Letter.
- In any case, it must never apply to specific indemnities, the tax indemnity or fundamental warranties.

## Part D: Price mechanics

### 17. Funds flow and the debt-free/cash-free definitions
**Why it matters**
- The Seller says the funds flow "reflects the agreed price mechanics" while leaving out the bonuses.

**Push back**
- Indebtedness and Transaction Expenses to expressly include:
  - the Riverlark payout, including break costs and fees;
  - the AUD 420,000 bonuses plus all on-costs;
  - the unpaid Ironquay AUD 180,000;
  - any related-party Sandbar amounts;
  - accrued but unpaid tax;
  - Seller transaction costs borne by the Company.
- Completion accounts or a locked-box Leakage covenant, as applicable, with a dollar-for-dollar indemnity.
- Consider a retention or escrow amount (for example 5 to 10%) for the known issues.
